t: The king was also priest, the figure between gods and people, and after death he was deified; the gods in turn were bound to provide for the people if they were worshipped properly.
The Hittites spoke of a thousand gods, many of them only names today, and many towns kept their own storm-gods instead of identifying them with one national figure.

Much that would give a balanced view is lost: there are no canonical scriptures and no theological discourses, and what is known rests on administrative tablets, carvings, seal stones and temple plans.
dyk: The Hittites sometimes worshipped their gods through Huwasi stones, which represented deities and were treated as sacred objects; gods were often shown standing on the backs of their animals.
ev: The Hittites create an empire centred in Anatolia, which lasts until about 1180 BCE
The queen and priestess Puduhepa works on organising and rationalising her people's religion
An inscription of Puduhepa invokes the sun goddess of Arinna, who in the land of Hatti has that name and in the land of cedars the name Hebat
The Hittite empire ends and its sites are finally burned
Beckman observes that many Hittite towns maintained individual storm-gods

f.origin: Anatolia, in the Hittite empire centred there from c. 1600 to 1180 BCE, with its capital at Hattusa; a mix of Hattian, Hurrian and Hittite influences
f.founder: none: a religion of a kingdom, drawing on Hattian, Hurrian and Mesopotamian traditions, with no single founder named
f.scriptures: no canonical scriptures: the surviving tablets are cult inventories, temple and ritual administration, diviners' reports, rituals and fragments of myth, some used in training scribes
f.followers: none: the religion ended with the Hittite empire c. 1180 BCE, when the Hittite sites were burned
